planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light with excellent drainage; variegation is strongest with more light but direct sun will scorch the thin cream margins. Trail from a hanging basket or train up a trellis or hoop.

directions: This classic variegated sport of the common wax plant bears thick, waxy, oval leaves edged in irregular bands of creamy white, with new growth often emerging flushed pink to rose before settling into green and cream. Clusters of small, fragrant, star-shaped pink-and-white flowers appear on mature vines, typically in warm months, releasing a sweet scent most noticeable in the evening. It climbs or trails on long, twining stems that are best supported on a trellis, hoop, or hanging basket. Let the chunky, well-draining potting mix dry out between waterings, since overwatering is the most common cause of root rot in this succulent-leaved vine.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light; variegated 'Splash' plants need more light than solid-green kerrii to maintain their flecking and grow more slowly as a result. Use a chunky, fast-draining aroid/succulent mix.

directions: A variegated form of the familiar heart-leaf hoya, 'Splash' carries the same thick, succulent, heart-shaped leaves but overlaid with irregular silvery-grey to pale-green flecks and speckles scattered across the deep green surface, with the pattern varying noticeably from leaf to leaf. Like its plain-green parent, single-leaf cuttings sold around Valentine's Day will root and persist for years but cannot produce new growth; a cutting with an intact node is needed to grow into a climbing vine. Mature, well-grown vines can produce clusters of small star-shaped flowers. Allow the potting mix to dry almost completely between waterings, since the thick leaves store water and are prone to rot if kept too wet.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, partially sunlit light in a hanging basket or on a trellis; both flowering and the intensity of the leaf variegation depend on light levels. Water sparingly and let the mix dry out between waterings.

directions: This fast-growing, large-leaved hoya bears broad, rounded, glossy green leaves marked with silvery to pale 'splash' flecking concentrated toward the leaf margins. A profuse bloomer compared to many hoya species, it produces rounded clusters of slightly fragrant pink flowers in summer when given enough light. It vines vigorously and is best grown on a trellis or allowed to scramble and trail from a hanging basket. Keep in a chunky, fast-draining mix and let it dry out between waterings, since the thick leaves hold reserves of water.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light (an east-facing window works well); allow the top two inches of chunky, well-draining aroid mix to dry before watering again.

directions: A striking hybrid philodendron grown for its long, narrow, deeply pinnate leaves with sharply serrated, saw-toothed margins that give the plant its reptilian common name. New leaves emerge flushed orange to pink before maturing to a bright lime-green to golden-yellow, a stable color that holds even as the leaves age and expand to several feet long on vigorous plants. It grows as a self-heading to semi-climbing aroid and benefits from staking or a moss pole as it matures and the leaves lengthen. Provide warm temperatures, high humidity, and a chunky bark-based mix, letting the top of the mix dry before the next watering.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light away from direct sun; Frost peperomia grows slowly and prefers evenly moist, well-drained potting mix that is never allowed to sit in standing water.

directions: A compact, upright cultivar of ripple peperomia prized for its deeply quilted, heart-shaped leaves, which emerge lime-green and mature to a frosty silver-grey with a mint-green base and contrasting darker green veining. The ruffled leaf texture catches light in a way that intensifies the silvery, frosted effect. Slender, upright, mouse-tail-like flower spikes rise above the compact rosette of foliage. Its small, tidy habit suits a windowsill, desk, or terrarium, and it propagates readily from leaf or stem cuttings rooted in moist soil.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, filtered light in a coarse, airy, well-drained epiphytic potting mix; this tough hybrid also tolerates lower light conditions better than many showy anthuriums.

directions: A bold, compact hybrid anthurium grown for its thick, broad, elliptical leaves with a quilted, deeply veined surface that reflects light in a dimensional, sculptural way. New leaves emerge bronze before hardening into a rich, glossy deep green, and the plant maintains a sturdy, upright, relatively compact profile even as it matures. It is considered easier-going and more forgiving of imperfect conditions than many of the showier velvet- and crystal-leaved anthurium species. Grow in a coarse, fast-draining aroid mix and let the top of the medium dry slightly before watering again.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in shadier, filtered light in a coarse, airy, well-drained epiphytic potting mix that allows air around the roots to help prevent rot.

directions: This full, bushy anthurium produces large, glossy, elliptical, lightly veined leaves on a vigorous, reliably clumping plant that quickly fills out a pot for a lush, jungle-like effect. In its native tropical forest habitat it grows epiphytically on trees, so it appreciates airflow around its roots and resents being kept constantly soggy. It is a tough, easygoing anthurium well suited to shadier rooms where more colorful anthurium species would struggle, and it takes well to division for propagation. Keep the coarse, bark-based potting mix evenly moist but never waterlogged.
